first_impression.reaction: My assistant opened it, saw a list of puns and a tip about searching tags before printing stationery, and summarised it in one line: 'consumer DIY piece, not relevant'. A public hashtag is the opposite of what we want. Our worry is photos getting out, not how to gather more of them. I only read further because she flagged the privacy section, and that part is sensible.

journey.quote: A good wedding hashtag is short, yours alone and easy for every guest to spell. You don't need a wedding hashtag generator to find one.
journey.reaction: Clear and quick, I'll give it that. But the first screen assumes everyone wants their wedding online. Nothing there tells me this brand thinks about families who don't.

journey.quote: and guests' photos shared the way you intend.
journey.reaction: That's the only line on the first screen that touches on control. It's too soft to keep me reading. 'Shared the way you intend' still takes for granted that things get shared.

journey.quote: **#HartsOffTheMarket:** cheeky, for a crowd that enjoys a joke.
journey.reaction: Fine for some couples. For us, a pun on the family name posted to strangers would be mortifying. It makes the brand feel aimed at a much more casual client.

journey.quote: A hashtag is public by design.
journey.reaction: Finally, the honest line. This is what my assistant would underline for me. I appreciate that it's said plainly and not dressed up.

journey.quote: So a tag suits photos you are happy for anyone to see. For everything else, a private shared album keeps the pictures among your guests.
journey.reaction: Sensible and understated. It's the right instinct. But it stops at 'pair it with an album'. It never says some families ask guests not to post at all, which is what we would do.

journey.quote: A line beside your hashtag on the welcome sign does a lot of work: please ask before you post anyone else, check with parents before sharing children, and we will remove any photo on request.
journey.reaction: Practical, and I like that removal on request is treated as normal. Asking politely and removing afterwards is still too loose for a family like ours, though. Once a photo is out, it's out, and the article admits that itself.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish.
journey.reaction: Competent, but generic. It says nothing about scale, exclusive use, security or keeping things off social media, which are the only things that would make me look twice.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD, and agrees the fee in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fees in writing is reassuring for a normal client. For me, leading with the fee and the currency feels transactional. I'm not asking what it costs at this stage, I'm asking what you can do.

unanswered_questions: Can the team set up and enforce a no-posting or phones-away policy for guests and suppliers?
Do suppliers and staff sign confidentiality agreements as standard?
Has Wedded Wonderland handled weddings of 200 to 400 guests, and multi-day events at that scale?
Can the team work with our own security and coordinate with a venue's security?
How are private guest albums controlled, and who has access to them?

turn_offs_found.quote: **#HartsOffTheMarket:** cheeky, for a crowd that enjoys a joke.
turn_offs_found.why: Jokey tone and puns on a family name read as mass-market. It tells me this brand's typical client is not like me.

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD, and agrees the fee in writing before any work begins.
turn_offs_found.why: Not discount talk, but leading the closing pitch with fee and currency feels like a package conversation, not a bespoke one.

cta_reaction.quote: Tell us your date, your guest list and where you would like to marry, and begin with [Wedded Concierge]
cta_reaction.why: I wouldn't enquire through a blog link on a hashtag article. We go through private channels or a referral. Nothing on this page shows discretion or experience at our scale, so it gives me no reason to ask for an introduction either.

top_3_changes: Old: "Below is that method, ideas by style built from invented couples, and what a list of tags can't settle: one tag across a weekend abroad, and guests' photos shared the way you intend." New: "Below is that method, ideas by style built from invented couples, and what a list of tags can't settle: one tag across a weekend abroad, and guests' photos shared the way you intend, including not shared publicly at all." Why: tells a privacy-first reader on the first screen that this page respects her choice.

Old: "If you would rather guests held off posting until after the ceremony, ask your celebrant to say so. That choice is yours." New: "If you would rather guests held off posting until after the ceremony, ask your celebrant to say so. Some couples go further and ask guests not to post at all, sharing a private album afterwards instead. That choice is yours." Why: names the option families like mine actually take, without any new claims about the brand.

Old: "Yes, as one option. A tag gives guests one place for public photos; for more privacy, pair it with a private album or skip it." New: "Yes, as one option. A tag gives guests one place for public photos; for more privacy, pair it with a private album, or skip the tag altogether and ask guests not to post." Why: makes the no-hashtag path explicit for anyone who values discretion over reach.

Does Wedded Wonderland have approved, sourced wording on discretion, confidentiality or large-scale delivery that could go in the Concierge CTA? I have not assumed any.
